extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science funders, and policy-makers interested in peer review and grant-rubric design
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding how covert reviewer criteria (institutional and cognitive particularism) shape grant decisions and how rubric and panel design can mitigate bias. Useful for those designing or auditing peer review processes for research funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional particularism — favoring prestigious institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring applicants from prestigious universities (e.g., Oxford, Cambridge, top US schools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travis & Collins identify preference for elite institutional affiliation as a covert criterion used by panels. This functions independently of the written criteria and can advantage applicants from well-known universities even when other merits are comparable. Audits of rubrics should account for institutional-affiliation effects, but note authors argue this form of particularism is less important than cognitive particularism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional particularism — favoring known applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring applicants known personally to panel members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal familiarity or network ties between applicants and reviewers operate as a biasing criterion. The study reports panels often reward those they know, which can subvert formal merit-based evaluation. Anti-patterns include relying on informal reputation signals rather than documented proposal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional particularism — favoring same departmental tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring applicants from the same departmental tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel members show partiality toward candidates embedded in their own departmental or institutional traditions. This can manifest as positive weighting for methods, topics, or training typical of the applicant's department. Rubrics should be designed to prevent undue advantage from shared departmental lineage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism — favoring reviewers' theoretical paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring proposals using reviewers' own theoretical paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors emphasize that reviewers systematically prefer proposals that align with their own theoretical commitments. This is often covert and shapes which proposals are judged as legitimate. Rubrics that do not surface these paradigm alignments risk excluding novel or paradigm-challenging work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism — favoring reviewers' methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring proposals using methodologies the reviewer practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers tend to privilege methods they themselves use, valuing familiar techniques and downrating unfamiliar ones irrespective of their suitability. This methodological parochialism can disadvantage interdisciplinary or methodologically innovative proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism — penalizing interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalizing interdisciplinary work that crosses paradigm boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinary proposals are often judged harshly because they sit between existing paradigms and do not fit reviewers' expectations of what 'counts' as the field. Travis & Collins report panels excluding or downgrading such work; rubric designers should explicitly evaluate interdisciplinary merit rather than allowing implicit paradigm-fit to determine quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism — penalizing heterodox or revolutionary research
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalizing heterodox or revolutionary research programs even when scientifically rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers give lower evaluations to work that challenges prevailing paradigms, favoring incremental 'normal science' contributions. The study documents systematic suppression of potentially paradigm-shifting proposals; rubrics should include protections (e.g., separate track, explicit criteria for novelty) to avoid penalizing rigorous heterodoxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism — favoring incremental/normal-science proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring incremental/normal-science proposals over Kuhnian revolutionary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an observed bias toward safer, incremental research that extends existing paradigms. This preference reduces the likelihood of funding transformative research. Evaluation frameworks should balance risk and potential impact rather than defaulting to incrementalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit boundary work — defining what 'counts' as the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit boundary work — defining what 'counts' as the field, and excluding what doesn't fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels perform boundary work that implicitly narrows the domain of acceptable proposals by excluding topics, methods, or perspectives judged outside the field. Such exclusionary practices operate as de facto criteria. Rubrics should make scope decisions explicit and justify exclusions to avoid covert gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition as a rubric-design choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel composition itself is a rubric-design choice with stronger effects than written criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travis & Collins argue that who sits on a panel (their paradigms, methods, networks) often determines outcomes more than the written rubric. Therefore, designing review processes requires deliberate choices about panel diversity of paradigms, methods, and institutional backgrounds; monitoring panel effects is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit requirement — surface and audit cognitive particularism
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rubric that does not surface and audit cognitive particularism will systematically suppress paradigm-shifting research, regardless of how it controls for institutional affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation from the study: rubrics and review processes must explicitly detect, disclose, and mitigate cognitive particularism (e.g., anonymization where possible, explicit criteria for evaluating paradigm-challenging work, diverse reviewer selection, separate assessment tracks). Failure to do so preserves covert biases that block novel science.
